1) both get weakened, but there is no intensity increase in any characteristic peak for
the newly formed compact β-phase at 200MV/m? In fact, the compact β-phase is
still β-phase. Is there any characteristic peak in the full FTIR spectrum for the
compact β-phase formed at a high field?
Response: Thank you for your thoughtful question. As reported in previous work [Adv.
Funct. Mater. 34, 2314705 (2024)], both the long-β phase (1275 cm-1) and short β-phase
(837 cm-1) absorption intensities in relaxor ferroelectric polymers such as P(VDF-TrFE-
CFE) are enhanced upon applying an electric field. This enhancement arises because
the G conformations can be converted into T conformations under the field, forming
longer T sequences. In particular, the three T units in each T3G segment polarize
cooperatively, eventually aligning as long-range all T sequences in the direction of the
electric field. This process reflects the dominance of T3G sequences in the terpolymer’s
response. In contrast, the PVDF-SPF films studied here were pretreated via uniaxial
stretching with a high strain of up to ~1400%, inducing a high content of long T chains
and yielding a β phase fraction of approximately 96%. This level remained largely
unchanged during the subsequent SPF process. Therefore, under an applied electric
field, the polarization response in PVDF-SPF involves the reorientation of pre-existing
β-phase dipoles, without the formation of new polar phases, which is distinct from the
field-induced phase transitions observed in terpolymers.
Fig. R15. Top-view schematic of the infrared transmission measurement of PVDF-SPF
under an electric field of 200 MV m-1. Characteristic absorption peaks of specific
functional groups appear in the infrared spectrum when the dipole moment vibration
direction lies in the incident plane.
Additionally, we wish to clarify the influence of the FTIR measurement mode. In the
transmission-mode FTIR setup used for PVDF-SPF, the infrared electric vector lies
perpendicular to the direction of propagation. When the direction of dipole moment
vibration lies within the incident plane, characteristic absorption peaks corresponding
to specific groups appear in the infrared spectrum. After applying the electric field, β-
phase dipoles tend to align with the field direction (i.e., parallel to the direction of
infrared light propagation), thereby reducing their projection along the direction of the
IR electric vector. As a result, the corresponding peak intensity decreases. The short-β
phase shows a similar trend. This behavior contrasts with that of terpolymers, where
field-induced β phase formation significantly increases the polar phase content and
enhances absorption intensity, effectively masking the reduction caused by dipole
reorientation. This behavior has also been confirmed in previous studies
[Macromolecules 54, 2334-2352 (2021); Macromolecules 45, 1954-1962 (2012)]. It
should be noted that, the term “compact β-phase” refers to a state of more tightly
aligned dipoles within the β-phase under electric field, rather than the formation of a
new crystalline phase. Therefore, no distinct characteristic peaks corresponding to this
compact β-phase have been observed in the full FTIR spectrum.
To address this comment, we have included this clarification in the revised manuscript
to explain that the observed IR response is attributed to dipole reorientation rather than
a phase transition. This distinction helps differentiate the behavior of PVDF-SPF from
that of relaxor terpolymers and highlights the structural origin of the electrocaloric
response in our system.
Revised Main Text: “Given the high β phase content (94%) in PVDF-SPF, further
increase in its concentration under the electric field is considered negligible. The
reduction in absorption intensity is primarily attributed to the reorientation of polar
dipoles along the field direction, which decreases their vibrational component along the
direction of the infrared electric vector (Supplementary Fig. 9).”
(Page 8, lines 186-191)

the PVDF-SPF film. The ΔT is calculated from the data measured by a heat flux sensor.
The curve does not show any platform but a large increasing rate even if the field is

max

fields. In the low-field region (<250 MV m-1), a large number of short-β phase structures
within the PVDF-SPF film can almost fully reorient along the applied field. The initial
polarization increase is primarily attributed to the activation of these loose and tiny β
crystals. As the field exceeds 250 MV m-1, the dipole alignment approaches saturation,
and the rate of polarization growth slows down significantly. This saturation is further
exacerbated by the limited structural flexibility between short-β phase regions and
amorphous chain segments, resulting in a “locked” microstructure that cannot respond
further to the field. This trend is also reflected in the behavior of the remanent
polarization (P). P represents the non-reversible component of the polarization that
r r
remains after the external field is removed. In the low-field region, as the field increases,
more short-β phase regions are aligned, and a small portion of dipoles remain oriented
after field removal, leading to a slight increase in P. However, above 250 MV m-1, P
r r
remains nearly constant, indicating that the reversible polarization component has been
nearly exhausted and the material begins to behave more like a linear dielectric.

cooling. This suggests that the material's polarization response is approaching
saturation in this field range, and thus, the potential for further ΔT improvement is
c
limited. Although the breakdown strength of the PVDF-SPF film is still far above the
maximum applied field, its effective polarization no longer increases significantly with
field strength. Therefore, we believe that the practical working limit for the
electrocaloric performance of PVDF-SPF lies in the 200-250 MV m-1 range. To fully
exploit the electrocaloric performance of PVDF-SPF without applying an excessively
high voltage, the operating electric field was set to 200 MV m-1.

approached saturation, and the polarization increase slowed markedly. The P remained
r
nearly constant, suggesting that the reversible polarization component was nearly
exhausted, and the material behavior became more linear (Supplementary Fig. 12).”
(Page 11, lines 239-242)
6. The 14.1K of ΔT at 200MV/m calculated from the heat flux sensor measurement is
a very large number. How does this compare to the ΔT measured using an IR camera
under the same condition?
Response: Thank you for your thoughtful question. We acknowledge that the original
manuscript did not provide a detailed characterization of the electrocaloric temperature
change (ΔT ) measured using an IR camera or infrared thermometer for the PVDF-SPF
c
film. We have supplemented time-resolved ΔT curves obtained using the IR
c
thermometer under various electric fields with a systematic comparison of the results
measured by the heat flux sensor. The comparison reveals that, under identical
conditions, the ΔT values recorded by the IR thermometer are lower than those
c
obtained from the heat flux sensor. Through further analysis, we have identified the
following primary factors that may contribute to this discrepancy:
(1) Difference in temporal resolution: The sampling interval of the IR thermometer
is approximately 100 ms, whereas the heat flux sensor has a response time of around
10 ms. Since the electrocaloric response of PVDF-SPF occurs within a short timescale
(a few tens of milliseconds) [Ferroelectrics 405, 26-31 (2010)], the IR thermometer
may fail to accurately capture the instantaneous peak temperature change, resulting in
an underestimation of ΔT .
c
(2) Thermal shielding caused by the CNT coating: To enhance the surface emissivity
for infrared detection, a layer of carbon nanotubes (CNTs) was sprayed onto the silver
electrodes. Although CNTs effectively improve emissivity, the coating thickness (~1
μm) could not be precisely controlled under the current experimental conditions. An
excessively thick CNT layer may partially absorb the released heat from the film,
leading to a lower apparent surface temperature measured by the IR thermometer.
Similar thermal shielding effects have also been reported in previous studies [Nat.
Commun. 15, 6670 (2024); Nature 640, 924-930 (2025)].
Fig. R16. ECE performance of the PVDF-SPF. a, Time-resolved heat flux signal of
PVDF-SPF. b, Time-resolved infrared thermometer signal of PVDF-SPF. c,
Comparison of the temperature change measured by the two methods.
To address this comment, we have further provided ΔT data obtained via the IR
c
thermometer at different temperatures and electric field strengths in the Supplementary
Information (Supplementary Fig. 5). Although the absolute temperature changes
measured by the IR thermometer are slightly lower, the observed field-dependent trends
are consistent with those obtained using the heat flux sensor. Corresponding
explanations have also been added to the main text and figure captions.
Revised Main Text: “This result was cross-validated using an infrared thermometer.
Due to lower sampling rates of the infrared method, the measured temperature change
was reduced (Supplementary Fig. 5b and 5c).”
(Page 6, lines 128-130)
7. Figure 2e shows that the ΔT of PVDF-SPF is almost negligible at 50-80MV/m. To
get a ΔT (at least 3-4 K) for practical cooling applications, the field needs to be at least
100MV/m which is not ideal for cooling device development. How does the ΔT scale
with film thickness? From the material standpoint, provide potential approaches to
obtain large ΔT at <100 MV/m.
Response: Thank you for your thoughtful question. We agree that the electrocaloric
temperature change (ΔT ) of PVDF-SPF under low electric fields (e.g., 50-80 MV m-1)
c
is relatively limited, which to some extent restricts its potential for low-voltage-driven
cooling device applications. One of the primary reasons for this limitation is the
relatively strong interchain interactions within the crystalline domains of PVDF-SPF.
When the polymer chains within a crystal are tightly packed and highly rigid, it
becomes difficult to achieve significant reversible dipole reorientation even under
increasing electric fields, thereby suppressing the resulting ΔT . Although our solid-
c
phase pressure forming (SPF) process has successfully transformed the β-phase crystals
into a looser structure with crystal sizes reduced to approximately 6 nm. This size is
close to the lower limit, where each crystal may contain only a few polymer chains
along the thickness direction. This “isolated crystalline domain” configuration is
beneficial for reducing interdomain coupling and enhancing polarizability, but it still
leaves room for improving chain-level dipolar flexibility under low electric fields.
We believe that the key to enhancing the electrocaloric response at low electric fields
lies in further weakening the interchain interactions within the crystalline regions,
thereby increasing the freedom of dipole orientation in weak fields. This could be
achieved by moderately increasing the interchain spacing (e.g., via fluorinated
monomer copolymerization or radiation-induced defects), or by increasing the distance
between highly polar units (e.g., through the incorporation of disulfonyl alkyl side
chains with a C3 spacer [Science 389, 69-72 (2025)]), while maintaining a small crystal
size.
In addition, to enhance the effective field strength acting on the crystalline regions,
we suggest re-designing the microstructure from the perspective of macroscopic
capacitor distribution. PVDF-based materials typically consist of crystalline and
amorphous domains, which can be simplified as a series connection of two capacitive
components with different dielectric constants. Since the dielectric constant of the
crystalline region is generally higher than that of the amorphous region, the external
electric field tends to concentrate in the amorphous phase, reducing the effective field
applied to the crystals. Therefore, optimizing the degree of crystallinity, constructing
interfaces with large polarization contrast, or introducing interfacial polar layers can
help redistribute the internal electric field more effectively toward the crystalline
regions. This redistribution facilitates stronger dipolar reorientation and enhances the
electrocaloric cooling performance even under low-voltage conditions.
To address this comment, we plan to further explore interchain-weakening molecular
strategies and multiscale structural designs that could enhance the low-field
electrocaloric performance. Relevant literature discussions and preliminary design
concepts have been added to the revised manuscript and Supplementary Information.
Reviewer #4 (Remarks to the Author):
This article introduces a novel method utilizing poly(vinylidene fluoride) (PVDF)
through solid-phase pressure forming (SPF) technology to enhance its electrocaloric
effect (ECE). The technique undergoes significant plastic deformation and extensive
crystal fragmentation in PVDF films, forming loose and tiny β-phase grains under 30
MPa solid-phase pressure. The remarkable ECE primarily originates from the entropy
change due to dipole swithing within molecular chains and the orientation entropy
change caused by reversible transitions between loose and compact β crystals. A high
electrocaloric temperature change of 14.1 K and a broad operational temperature
window of 60 °C are achieved at room temperature. Overall, the work demonstrates a
highly novel approach. I recommend addressing several issues before acceptance of this
paper.
1. In the introduction part, the author declared they are obtaining more “extended-chain
beta crystal”, however, WAXD result showed the crystalline size only 6.22 nm, I
recommend the author to verify by SAXS, or another way is to delete the incorrect
calling of “ECC”.
Response: Thank you for your valuable suggestion. We agree with the reviewer’s
assessment regarding the crystal size. We also realize that referring to the structure as
an “extended-chain β crystal” could be confusing, considering the crystalline size of
only 6.22 nm observed by WAXD. We intended to highlight the formation of more
extended all-trans chain conformations during original stretching, rather than
conventional extended-chain crystals with much larger crystalline sizes. We also
recognize that the molecular chain length is not equivalent to the crystalline size, and
therefore this expression is indeed inaccurate.
To address this comment, we have removed the terms “extended-chain β crystal” and
“ECC” from the revised manuscript and clarified the relevant content to avoid potential
ambiguity.
Revised Main Text: “Upon uniaxial stretching for PVDF-C, the α and γ spherulites can
transform into fibrous β crystals with electroactivity, which are mainly used as
piezoelectric materials with a piezoelectric coefficient typically between 20 and 35 pC
N-1.”
(Page 5, lines 109-112)
2. In the in situ 2D-WAXD experiments, changes in β-crystal size and interchain
spacing are clearly reported. Have the authors also quantified any change in overall
crystallinity? If so, what is the magnitude of this change under applied electric field,
and what physical processes—such as field-induced recrystallization or partial
melting—might drive it?
Response: Thank you for your thoughtful question. We acknowledge that the
quantitative analysis of crystallinity from the in situ 2D-WAXD data under the electric
field was missing in the original manuscript. As shown in Fig. 2e, the diffraction
intensity of the β crystal becomes more pronounced after applying the electric field,
while the scattering intensity in the amorphous region (around 18.5°) slightly decreases.
Based on the circular integral intensity profiles of the 2D-WAXD patterns, we found
that the overall crystallinity increases by approximately 4% under the applied field.
This suggests that some amorphous chain segments became more ordered and
transformed into loosely packed β crystal structures. This transformation is not a
conventional recrystallization process, as the temperature remains constant during the
application of the electric field, and no new diffraction peaks are observed in the WAXD
patterns. Instead, we believe it results from field-induced conformational reordering of
chain segments, particularly within the interfacial transition regions formed after solid-
phase pressure forming. In these regions, the disparity in interchain spacing between
crystalline and amorphous zones is significantly reduced. As a result, some chain
segments exhibit quasi-crystalline behavior and respond more readily to the applied
field by forming polar-ordered structures, which enhances the polarization response.
Fig. R17. Change in circular integral crystallinity of PVDF-SPF before and after
applying the electric field. The shaded area in the curve represents the loss associated
with the reversible β crystal transition, similar to a hysteresis loop. The circular integral
crystallinity is obtained by integrating the 2D-WAXD pattern over the full 360°
azimuthal angle. This amplifies the contribution from the amorphous regions and leads
to an underestimated crystallinity. The crystallinity of PVDF-SPF was calculated based
on the DSC crystallization melting enthalpy value of 54.6 J g-1, resulting in a
crystallinity of 52.8 % (theoretical enthalpy for fully crystalline PVDF is 103.4 J g-1).
To address this comment, we have added a quantitative analysis of the crystallinity
change before and after electric field application in the revised manuscript. The relevant
discussion has been included in the “Reversible transition in β crystals” section.
Revised Main Text: “After applying a high voltage, the molecular chains in PVDF-SPF
became more compact (Fig. 2f), resulting in a decrease in D, accompanied by an
increase in relative crystallinity (Supplementary Fig. 10).”
(Page 9, lines 213-215)
3. The dielectric constant of all three films (PVDF-SPF, PVDF-C, and PVDF-S) was
measured in range of 0 to 140 °C. It is reasonable to see the decrease after 80 °C,
however, I recommend the authors to carry out dielectric constant measurement to
below the glass transition (i.e., -40°C), It seems that the high dielectric constant is
original from the orientation of the amorphous phase, i.e., the orientated amorphous
fraction (OAF).
Response: Thank you for your valuable suggestion. We have added the temperature-
dependent dielectric spectra of PVDF-SPF films in the range of -80 °C to 30 °C. The
results show a significant increase in both the dielectric constant and loss near the glass
transition temperature (approximately -30 °C). This phenomenon resembles the
polarization enhancement mechanism proposed in previous work [J. Mater. Chem. C 9,
894-907 (2021)], which is attributed to the formation of an oriented amorphous fraction
(OAF). Therefore, we believe that a similar OAF-like structure may also form in the
PVDF-SPF films. However, it should be noted that the primary focus of the referenced
study was the enhancement of piezoelectric performance, while our work centers on
improving the ECE. These two properties rely on distinct dipole behaviors: the
piezoelectric effect depends more on a stable and highly oriented dipole alignment,
whereas the ECE requires dipoles to respond reversibly to an applied electric field.
Although we observed enhanced dielectric response and low-temperature
polarization in the PVDF-SPF samples, which implies the possible presence of a certain
level of order within the amorphous structure, we tend to regard it as an “intermediate
phase” structure [J. Polym. Sci., Part B: Polym. Phys. 32, 2289-2306 (1994)]. This
hypothesis requires further validation through detailed microstructural
characterizations. As this study primarily aims to clarify the relationship between
structure and ECE performance, we did not elaborate on the OAF mechanism. We
believe that this direction holds substantial potential for future investigations,
particularly in exploring the influence of OAF-like structures on ECE responses.
Fig. R18. a, Dielectric constant and b, dielectric loss spectra of PVDF-SPF in the range
of -80 °C to 30 °C.
To address this comment, we have added the above discussion into the revised
manuscript under the “Temperature-dependent ECE behavior” section. This addition
introduces the concept of “intermediate phases” and briefly compares their polarization
behavior with that reported in previous studies.
Revised Main Text: “At low temperatures (approximately −30 °C), both k and dielectric
loss increased significantly (Supplementary Fig. 18a and 18d). This behavior resembles
the polarization enhancement mechanism reported previously. The structure in PVDF-
SPF, referred to as loose β crystals (similar to intermediate phases), can greatly improve
the reversible ECE.”
(Page 12, lines 272-277)
4. Again, if the above assumption is true, then the OAF should also significantly
enhance the ECE performance, the authors should discuss this effect in the manuscript.
Response: Thank you for your valuable suggestion. We agree that, as the reviewer
suggested, if the high dielectric constant originates from the oriented amorphous
fraction (OAF), this structure may also contribute positively to the ECE performance.
Previous studies have shown that OAF structures can be introduced through processing
methods such as stretching and electrical poling [Mater. Horiz. 9, 1992-1998 (2022)],
and they have a significant influence on polarization behavior and electromechanical
performance. In future work, we plan to conduct detailed structural characterizations to
further verify the specific role of OAF in enhancing ECE properties.
To address this comment, we have added relevant background information in the
Introduction section of the revised manuscript to discuss the potential contribution of
OAF structures to polarization behavior and field-induced responses. We believe that
this addition helps to better highlight the potential role of OAF structures in enhancing
ECE performance. The changes in the revised manuscript are as follows:
Revised Main Text: “In addition, high-power ultrasonication was utilized to induce a
hard-to-soft transition, increasing the piezoelectric coefficient d in PVDF19. The
31
presence of oriented amorphous fraction structures has been reported to greatly improve
the piezoelectric response of PVDF20. This suggests that such “intermediate phases”
with ordered conformations may significantly contribute to the polarization behavior.”
(Page 3, lines 69-74)
I co-reviewed this manuscript with one of the reviewers who provided the listed
reports. This is part of the Nature Communications initiative to facilitate training in peer review
and to provide appropriate recognition for Early Career Researchers who co-review
manuscripts.
Reviewer #5 (Remarks to the Author):
This paper presents an enhanced electrocaloric effect (ECE) in poly(vinylidene fluoride)
(PVDF) homopolymer subjected to solid-state pressure forming. Given the low cost
and wide availability of PVDF homopolymer, the reported findings are noteworthy and
have the potential to stimulate further research of ECE in PVDF homopolymer. I
recommend the publication of this paper.
However, I have concerns regarding the high Joule heating observed, as shown in
Supplementary Figures 2(c) and 3(a), which may limit the practical applications of the
reported material for electrocaloric cooling devices. Despite this limitation, I feel this
work will inspire future research of ECE on PVDF homopolymer that may lead to
practical (and low cost) electrocaloric cooling materials. The authors may consider
(optional) adding one or two sentences in Supplementary Information about this Joule
heating when discussing Supplementary Figures 2(c) and 3(a).
Response: Thank you for your valuable suggestion. We fully understand the impact of
Joule heating on the performance of ECE cooling devices, especially under high electric
fields, which may indeed limit the practical application of the material. In our ECE
measurements, the PVDF-SPF films had a thickness of approximately 10 μm and were
cut into 15 × 15 mm squares. Silver electrodes with diameters of 6 mm and 8 mm were
uniformly deposited on both surfaces, and conductive silver paste with fine silver wires
was used for electrical connection. Under typical testing conditions (with the entire
ECE cycle lasting ~12 seconds and the high electric field applied for only 6 seconds),
the intrinsically high resistivity of PVDF generally prevented noticeable Joule heating
or dielectric breakdown. However, we did observe that a few samples exhibited
asymmetric thermal behavior, where the heat released during field application was
greater than the heat absorbed during field removal. We attribute this to possible factors
such as non-uniform electrode coating, local poor contact of the silver paste, or
undetected local degradation. Therefore, we fully acknowledge that the Joule
heating effect raised in your comment must be carefully identified and minimized
during ECE measurements.
Fig. R19. a, Time-resolved heat flux signal of PVDF-SPF. b, ECE signal of PVDF-SPF
measured by the heat flux sensor under 200 MV m-1. The red shaded area represents
the Joule heating of the film during field application, while the blue shaded area
indicates the electrocaloric cooling upon field removal. Mild Joule heating was
observed under high electric fields, possibly caused by leakage currents associated with
enhanced polarization, which may slightly reduce the electrocaloric cooling. This issue
could be alleviated through further optimization of material processing or device design.
To address this comment, we repeated the measurements on several other samples
from the same batch. The results showed that most samples did not exhibit similar
overheating behavior, confirming that the previously reported data reflected an isolated
anomaly. As a result, we have removed the anomalous data from the revised manuscript
and updated the ECE temperature change curves and associated temperature values to
better represent the intrinsic ECE behavior. In addition, we have added a brief
discussion on potential thermal sources in both the main manuscript and the
Supplementary Information. Strategies such as electrode optimization, improved
interface bonding, and voltage reduction are proposed to help suppress undesired
thermal effects in future applications.
Revised Main Text: “Optimizing electrode design, improving interface bonding, and
reducing operating voltage could effectively suppress this effect.”
(Page 26, lines 594-595)

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
The authors have provided substantial additional experiments to support their claim. The revised interpretations resolve the methodological and consistency issues I raised.
The consistent contrast in temperature changes measured by the heat flux sensor and IR camera via the highly emissive surface is very interesting – it suggests a systematic discrepancy between the two methods, which the authors attributed to the difference in the frame rate. If this claim were true, it would then lead to two important implications: 1) the cooling power within those tens of milliseconds time in difference would be large and thus promising for heat pump applications; 2) such large cooling power may now only be consumed by the inactive mass of the current film geometry, and thus the effective temperature change for useful heat transfer would be small. Therefore, for future development of EC heat pumps with large cooling powers and real-world relevance, it would be important to study EC materials as working bodies with large active thermal mass, presumably in the form of multilayer capacitors, either in planar [Appl. Phys. Lett. 102, 122904 (2013)] or roller configurations.
I therefore suggest the publication of this manuscript, and encourage the authors to consider my comment above for further improvements.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The revised manuscript has addressed some of my concerns. However, the phenomenon of "loosely packed beta phase enhances the ECE" was not first presented by this work. This work identified another method that could achieve a similar polar structure to enhance the ECE in PVDF (it is good enough). The authors should acknowledge the contribution of the prior work (Ref.11) and focus the report on their own innovations. Therefore, it is these authors who made me quote this in Ref.11, "The large number of newly formed, small-sized polar entities adopted a loosely correlated, high-entropy state, as suggested by DSC and XRD results." And currently, the narrative still seems to suggest it is they who discovered this phenomenon. And when they cite the ref. 11, there is no discussion on this phenomenon. The scientific origin of this work lies in achieving the polar structure "in PVDF". Without correctly acknowledging the contribution of prior work, this manuscript can be misleading to potential readers about its true significance.
From the revision, I still cannot understand why 97.2 J USD-1 is a meaningful value. The value only means something if the EC device is available for purchase in the market. If the authors still want to argue this is outstanding, they should compare it with that of the gaseous refrigerant that is currently available on-shelf.
In addition, the Joule heating is still significant. If 97.2 J USD-1 is outstanding, how about the additional cost of the additional size of heat sink that has to be there due to the additional heat generated and accumulated during each cycle? It will be a misleading point in this field from the device's point of view. I would suggest the authors not to discuss this, or they have to give a full picture of the economic view of EC technology, which is not really necessary for highlighting the key innovation of this work.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3: The following is my perspective on the author’s response to reviewer #3. Right now, my primary concern lies in the large discrepancy between ΔTcs measured with the heat flux sensor and those measured with the IR thermometer. The ΔTc measured with the heat flux sensor is even more than three times that measured with the IR thermometer under the same field. Frankly speaking, it is very unlikely that the device’s capturing frequency and the emissivity can account for this significant difference. In fact, a film with a temperature change of 14.2 K (now has been changed to 12.8 K) far exceeds the requirements for the commercialization of this solid-state cooling material (assuming that the stability issue is neglected). It is very good to present the comparison of ΔTcs measured with the two different methods. However, a statement of an exact 12.8 K temperature change might not be suitable.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_4: The author has fully addressed my concerns, thus I recommend the manuscript to be published in Nat. Commun.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_5: The authors have addressed my question, and I suggest accepting this paper.

Response to the Reviewers’ Comments
From negligible to giant electrocaloric effect of poly(vinylidene fluoride)
(NCOMMS-25-05580-A)
Dear Reviewers:
Thank you again for your valuable comments and suggestions on our manuscript. We
have carefully considered all the comments. The main revisions include additional
experiments, supplementary analyses, and adjustments to relevant expressions, which
are explained in detail in the point-by-point responses. All changes are highlighted in
red in the revised manuscript.
Best regards
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
The consistent contrast in temperature changes measured by the heat flux sensor and
IR camera via the highly emissive surface is very interesting – it suggests a systematic
discrepancy between the two methods, which the authors attributed to the difference in
the frame rate. If this claim were true, it would then lead to two important implications:
1) the cooling power within those tens of milliseconds time in difference would be large
and thus promising for heat pump applications; 2) such large cooling power may now
only be consumed by the inactive mass of the current film geometry, and thus the
effective temperature change for useful heat transfer would be small. Therefore, for
future development of EC heat pumps with large cooling powers and real-world
relevance, it would be important to study EC materials as working bodies with large
active thermal mass, presumably in the form of multilayer capacitors, either in planar
[Appl. Phys. Lett. 102, 122904 (2013)] or roller configurations.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for the in-depth analysis and constructive
comments on our work. We agree with the reviewer’s inference that the instantaneous
cooling power could be significant. Still, in the current film structure, it is likely
dissipated by the inactive thermal mass (such as the electrode mass and the high-
emissivity coating), thereby reducing the effective temperature change. The focus of
this study was to reveal the structural origin and response process of the large
electrocaloric effect in homopolymer PVDF. For this reason, the instantaneous cooling
power was not further quantified. We consider the reviewer’s suggestion on future
investigations with working bodies of larger effective thermal mass (such as multilayer
capacitors, roller configurations, electrostatic-driven devices, and self-regenerative

review_generation.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Poly(vinylidene fluoride) (PVDF), the most widely used ferroelectric polymer, typically exhibits a negligible electrocaloric effect (ECE) due to its symmetrical molecular configuration and bulky ferroelectric domains. PVDF-based ferroelectric terpolymers with giant ECE are expensive and have a narrow temperature window (Tw). Here, we report that PVDF films prepared by solid-phase pressure forming (PVDF-SPF) show a giant ECE of up to 12.8 K at 25 °C and a wide Tw of 60 °C. PVDF films underwent significant plastic deformation and extensive crystal fragmentation, forming loose and tiny β crystal grains under 30 MPa solid-phase pressure. The giant ECE primarily originates from orientation entropy changes of molecular chains associated with the reversible transition between loose and compact β crystals, as well as switching entropy changes of polar dipoles in tiny grains. Given the availability of PVDF, this work opens a route for the development of scalable solid-state cooling techniques.

---

## Introduction

Our society heavily relies on cooling technologies, such as air conditioning, with the traditional vapor compression cycle being the dominant method. However, this technology suffers from low energy efficiency, large volume, and high complexity. Furthermore, there is an intensifying environmental concern regarding the ozone-depleting and greenhouse gas-emitting refrigerants utilized in vapor compression systems1. Solid-state cooling technologies based on caloric effects offer promising alternatives with superior energy efficiency and zero emissions2. Caloric effects can be classified into magnetocaloric3,4, mechanocaloric5–9 and electrocaloric effect10–12 according to the action of external fields. Electrocaloric cooling shows potential for applications in human thermoregulation, battery thermal management, energy harvesting and refrigeration13. To date, refrigerants with both high ECE and low cost remain a significant technical challenge for the large-scale application of electrocaloric cooling.

Entropy changes stemming from conformational transitions and dipole orientations are the main contributors to the ECE temperature drop (ΔTECE) in polymers14. PVDF-based ferroelectric terpolymers, such as poly(vinylidene fluoride-trifluoroethylene-chlorotrifluoroethylene) [P(VDF-TrFE-CTFE)], are well-studied relaxor ferroelectric terpolymers in electrocaloric. The large volume and physical pinning effect of the comonomers in the terpolymer restrict the ferroelectric domains to the nanoscale, creating polar nanoregions. The nanoregions facilitate filed-induced relaxor ferroelectric to ferroelectric conformation transitions, resulting in a slim hysteresis loop15,16. The non-polar phase of the terpolymer transform into the polar β phase when an electric field was applied, confirming that its ECE is primarily attributable to the structural phase transition11. The reversible reorientation of the molecular chain conformation contributes to the large entropy and temperature change of terpolymers17.

Despite the superior ferroelectricity of PVDF, it exhibits negligible ECE at room temperature due to bulky and compact ferroelectric domains, which result from its symmetrical and regular molecular configuration. To improve its electrical performance, strategies such as repeated pressing-and-folding have been employed to extend polymer chains multidirectionally, thereby boosting dielectric energy storage capability18. In addition, high-power ultrasonication was utilized to induce a hard-to-soft transition, increasing the piezoelectric coefficient d31 in PVDF19. The presence of oriented amorphous fraction structures has been reported to greatly improve the piezoelectric response of PVDF20. In polymers, the introduction of a small number of double bonds can generate numerous loosely correlated polar entities in a high-entropy state, which also favor the ECE11. This suggests that such loosely correlated intermediate phases with ordered conformations may significantly contribute to the polarization behavior. In general, the morphology of polymers is influenced by both chain structure and processing techniques21,22. We believe that optimized forming techniques can restrict the ferroelectric domains of PVDF to tiny grains with loosely assembled chains. Given that the dipole moment of the PVDF monomer is higher than that of the comonomers in PVDF-based terpolymer23,24, the maximum polarization (Pmax) of PVDF is consequently higher. Therefore, PVDF has the potential to exhibit giant ECE if the bulky polar dipoles are decoupled.

Here, we first performed uniaxial stretching for the PVDF films prepared by solvent casting (PVDF-C), achieving a stretched PVDF film (PVDF-S) with 96% β crystal. This process increased the long-range order while minimizing the initial dipole switching entropy, resulting in an entropic storage effect. The entropic storage effect boosted the piezoelectricity of PVDF but inhibited the ECE25. Subsequently, the PVDF-S underwent significant plastic deformation and extensive crystal fragmentation during solid-phase pressure forming (SPF), a pressure-forming method below the melting temperature of materials, to form PVDF-SPF film. The SPF technology exhibited a super entropic effect, effectively releasing the entropy stored during the stretching process. The variable-angle attenuated total reflection infrared (VA-IR) spectra revealed the internal orientation of the β phase. The atomic force microscopy with infrared spectroscopy (AFM-IR) images proved the decoupling of long-range order in the molecular chains of PVDF-SPF. In situ high-voltage infrared spectra confirmed the reversibility of dipole flipping, and in situ high-voltage 2D wide-angle X-ray diffraction (2D-WAXD) curves illustrated the reversible transition between loose and compact β crystals. The PVDF-SPF achieved a giant ΔTECE of 12.8 K at 25 °C and 200 MV m−1 (breakdown field strength, Eb = 617 MV m−1), surpassing PVDF-C by 20 times. The PVDF-SPF displayed a wide Tw of 60 °C and a high Young’s modulus (Y) of 1.7 GPa, demonstrating excellent overall performance and application potential.

---

## Results

Solid-phase pressure formed PVDF for ECE
The PVDF-C is dominated by α and γ spherulites with large and weakly polar paraelectric dipole domains26 (Fig. 1a), which is mainly used as dielectric materials27. The PVDF-C demonstrates a slender hysteresis loop28 with a Pmax generally around 2 μC cm−2 at 200 MV m−1. Upon uniaxial stretching for PVDF-C, the α and γ spherulites can transform into fibrous β crystals with electroactivity29, which are mainly used as piezoelectric materials with a piezoelectric coefficient25 typically between 20 and 35 pC N−1. However, the ECE of these piezoelectric materials is generally poor. To achieve a giant ECE in PVDF, it is essential to maximize the β phase to increase the density of field-induced dipoles. Uniaxial stretching of PVDF-C to a strain of up to 1400% (Fig. 1b) yielded PVDF-S with approximately 96% β phase (Supplementary Note 1), forming fibrous β crystals with bulky and compact ferroelectric dipoles. Subsequently, the PVDF-S was gradually pressurized to 30 MPa at 85 °C by a hot press machine with adhesive gaskets for primary SPF. At 155 °C, we applied the same pressurization method for secondary SPF. The processes cause the film to undergo significant plastic deformation along the transverse direction (Fig. 1d) and extensive β crystal fragmentation, destroying the long-range ordered structure and forming loose and tiny β grains (Fig. 1c). The β phase content of PVDF-SPF was reduced to 94% (Supplementary Fig. 1).

The PVDF-C showed a negligible ΔTECE of 0.6 K. The PVDF-S exhibited a limited ΔTECE of 1.9 K, predicting a small amount of crystal fragmentation in the film by high-draw ratio stretching. The PVDF-SPF demonstrated a significantly higher ECE, with a maximum ΔTECE of 12.8 K at 25 °C and 200 MV m−1 (Fig. 1e and Supplementary Figs. 3 and 5a). This result was cross-validated using an infrared thermometer. Due to lower sampling rates of the infrared method, the measured temperature change was reduced (Supplementary Fig. 5). A high-resolution infrared thermal imager visually captured the temperature variations of the PVDF-SPF during a single electrocaloric cycle, confirming the giant electrocaloric effect (Fig. 1f and Supplementary Movie 1).

To investigate the intrinsic relationship between ECE and crystal morphology, we employed VA-IR30 to characterize the orientation and distribution of the β phase in PVDF membranes prepared by three processing methods (Supplementary Fig. 2). VA-IR is a characterization technique that captures conformational information across all azimuthal angles by rotating the film sample. This enables in situ visualization of the spatial distribution of molecular conformations within the film. The PVDF-C primarily contained the short-γ phase16 (at 833 cm−1), which displayed weak electroactivity and showed strong vibrational signals at all angles (Fig. 1g). Almost no intensity of the long-β phase16 (at 1275 cm−1) was observed. The PVDF-S revealed a strong long-β phase signal at all angles, while the short-β phase16 (at 837 cm−1) presented a pronounced signal near 0° (Fig. 1h). This observation indicated that the molecular chains in the PVDF-S possessed predominant regular long-range ordered structure with limited short-range ordering. The longer all-trans conformation necessitates a higher electric field strength for alignment with the field direction31, which impedes dipole orientation and reduces the switching entropy change during flipping.

The PVDF-SPF presented a distinct β phase distribution compared to the PVDF-S. The long-β phase became discontinuous, while the short-β phase became continuous at all angles, indicating an interruption of long-range order (Fig. 1i). The spectral width of the electroactive short-β phase increased, suggesting a greater variety of microscopic polar states and a more disordered short-β phase orientation32. Additionally, across the entire angle, the difference between the maximum and minimum intensities of the short-β phase decreased, suggesting to a more uniform distribution. Thus, the number of microscopic polar states in the PVDF-SPF was dramatically increased, which enhanced the dipole switching entropy change (ΔSdip) and positively impacted the ECE of the system.

Reversible transition in β crystals
To facilitate a more direct observation of the polar conformational distribution in the three films, we characterized the samples using AFM-IR33. An infrared wavelength of 1275 cm−1, associated with the all-trans conformation of PVDF, was selected for analysis34. The topographies of the films were measured, and the nanoscale infrared images were normalized to more clearly delineate the β phase distribution (Supplementary Fig. 6).

The surface morphology of PVDF-C exhibited spherical aggregation (Supplementary Fig. 6a), with a quite weak intensity of the all-trans conformation and only discernible in specific regions (Fig. 2a). In contrast, the PVDF-S displayed a clear molecular chain orientation, as evidenced by stretching marks on the surface (Supplementary Fig. 6b). The oriented molecular chains aggregated, reaching a width of approximately 730 nm (Fig. 2b). The infrared amplitude for all-trans conformation was observably enhanced, indicating strong long-range coupling. Despite the presence of oriented molecular chains in the PVDF-SPF, the long-range coupling was disrupted. The aggregation width of the short all-trans conformation was reduced to 150 nm (Fig. 2c), with a more uniform distribution and increased orientational randomness. This result was highly consistent with the measurements obtained from VA-IR (Fig. 1i). The peak intensities of the infrared amplitude for the PVDF-S and PVDF-SPF were 0.64 mV and 0.6 mV, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 6d), without a significant decrease in the molecular chain polarity during SPF. Additionally, Young’s modulus (Y) was characterized by AFM (Supplementary Fig. 7), with values of 1.1, 2.1, and 1.7 GPa for PVDF-C, PVDF-S, and PVDF-SPF, respectively. High modulus could notably improve the mechanical performance and fatigue durability of polymer electrocaloric devices.

Moreover, we employed high-voltage infrared spectroscopy (Supplementary Fig. 8) to analyze the evolution of internal polar conformation in the PVDF-SPF17,35. After applying 200 MV m−1 to PVDF-SPF, the infrared absorption of both the long-β phase and the short-β phase weakened (Fig. 2d). Given the high β phase content (94%) in PVDF-SPF, further increase in its concentration under the electric field is considered negligible. The reduction in absorption intensity is primarily attributed to the reorientation of polar dipoles along the field direction, which decreases their vibrational component along the direction of the infrared electric vector36,37 (Supplementary Fig. 9). This reorientation also leads to a decrease in dipolar entropy (Supplementary Note 3). The initial spectrum of PVDF-SPF was nearly identical to that after high-voltage removal, confirming the reversibility of the dipole flipping. Subsequently, high-voltage 2D WAXD characterization was performed (Fig. 2g)36. The peak position of PVDF-SPF shifted from 20.15° to 20.48°, decreasing the interchain spacing of the β crystal (Fig. 2e). The dispersion of the Debye ring reflects the orientational disorder among β crystals. A broad and diffuse ring indicates more random orientation, corresponding to a more disordered system with higher entropy. In contrast, a sharp and concentrated ring suggests increased orientational order and lower entropy. Based on this observation, we propose that changes in the orientational order of crystal domains may represent an additional and previously overlooked entropy contribution, namely the β phase orientation entropy change (ΔSorient) (detailed derivation in Supplementary Note 3). The degree of chain compactness, the orientation of molecular chains, and the quantity of β grains all affect the microstate number in the crystal morphology, leading to the corresponding entropy, known as β phase orientation entropy. The ΔSorient can be calculated using Boltzmann’s entropy equation:

ΔSorient = kB (N ln ΔΩD + ln ΔΩP) (1)

where kB is the Boltzmann constant, ΔΩD, ΔΩP and N represented the changes in microstates due to interchain spacing (D), chain orientation (P) and β grain quantity (N), respectively. The broadening of 837 cm−1 in the VA-IR characterization (Fig. 1i) indicated that the initial PVDF-SPF had a large microstate number in the short-β phase. AFM-IR images (Fig. 2c) showed that lower β phase orientation corresponded to greater randomness. After applying a high voltage, the molecular chains in PVDF-SPF became more compact (Fig. 2f), resulting in a decrease in D, accompanied by an increase in relative crystallinity (Supplementary Fig. 10). The narrowed diffraction rings (Fig. 2g) indicated an increase in P. These changes significantly reduced the microstate number of the system, leading to a decrease in entropy.

Upon removal of the electric field, an entropy increase occurred. Moreover, a tinier crystal size implies a larger N, with small changes in ΔΩD and ΔΩP leading to a great ΔSorient. The minor shaded areas signified that the transition from loose to compact β crystal resulted in a negligible loss (Fig. 2f). As with ΔSdip, the orientation entropy was reversible under the electric field.

Electrical responses and structural analysis
We performed various electrical and structural characterizations on PVDF-C, PVDF-S and PVDF-SPF. The PVDF-C exhibited a slim polarization-electric field hysteresis loop (P-E loop), with a Pmax of only 1.86 μC cm−2 at 200 MV m−1 (Fig. 3a), insufficient for providing adequate switching entropy. The PVDF-S showed a fat P-E loop (Fig. 3b), with a high Pmax of 9.83 μC cm−2 and a large remanent polarization (Pr) of 5.85 μC cm−2 at 200 MV m−1, indicative of piezoelectricity38. However, the permanent dipoles with high density, which are proportional to large Pr, failed to follow electric field variations, sacrificing both ΔSdip and the ECE. In contrast, the PVDF-SPF displayed a distinctly different P-E loop (Fig. 3c and Supplementary Fig. 11) with a high Pmax of 9.13 μC cm−2 and a low Pr of 1.12 μC cm−2 at 200 MV m−1, favoring a high ΔSdip and a giant ECE. The unipolar P-E loop efficiency of PVDF-SPF was much higher than that of PVDF-S and comparable to that of the linear dielectric PVDF-C (Fig. 3d), explaining the excellent reversibility of ECE cycling for PVDF-SPF. This was further confirmed by the large electrostriction of up to 5% under 200 MV m−1 (Supplementary Fig. 13). When the field exceeded 250 MV m−1, dipole alignment approached saturation, and the polarization increase slowed markedly. The Pr remained nearly constant, suggesting that the reversible polarization component was nearly exhausted, and the material behavior became more linear (Supplementary Fig. 12).

To gain a more profound comprehension of the effects of processing temperature on the structure of PVDF-SPF, we examined the crystalline morphology using 2D-WAXD (Supplementary Fig. 14). The PVDF-SPF subjected only to low-temperature SPF at 85 °C (PVDF-SPF85) exhibited the same 2θ angle of 20.52° (β crystals, 200/110 plane39) as PVDF-S, but with a dramatically broader full width at half maximum. The crystallite size reduced to 6.22 nm (Supplementary Fig. 14f). In addition, the crystalline melting enthalpy of PVDF-SPF85 (54.8 J g−1) also be lower than that of PVDF-S (61.3 J g−1) (Supplementary Fig. 15c). The above results show that low-temperature SPF mainly crushed larger β crystals, decoupled polar dipoles and increase ΔSdip.

After further high-temperature SPF at 155 °C, the 2θ angle of PVDF-SPF decreased from 20.52° (PVDF-SPF85) to 20.16° without new peaks (Fig. 3e). The interchain spacing increased to 4.41 Å (Supplementary Fig. 14f). The DSC melting range of PVDF-SPF expanded from 13.2 °C (PVDF-SPF85) to 17.1 °C (Fig. 3f and Supplementary Fig. 15d). These results demonstrated that high-temperature SPF increased the polydispersity of the β crystals and expanded the molecular chain spacing within the β crystals, creating ΔSorient from loose to compact β crystals.

We then conducted measurements of the dielectric properties of the films. Both stretching and SPF methods increased the dielectric constant (k) of PVDF films, with PVDF-SPF exhibiting the highest k of 19.2 at 1 kHz (Supplementary Fig. 16a). The stretching process enhanced the number of polar dipoles and improved electroactivity. The SPF process decoupled larger polar dipoles, facilitating dipole flipping and increasing the k. Additionally, the PVDF-SPF achieved a higher Eb (617 MV m−1) (Supplementary Fig. 16b), making it suitable for higher voltage ECE devices.

Temperature-dependent ECE behavior
It was crucial to explore the effective Tw of PVDF-SPF. To this end, we systematically study the dielectric response of three films using variable-temperature dielectric spectroscopy (Supplementary Fig. 17). Compared to PVDF-C and PVDF-S, the k of PVDF-SPF increased with temperature (Fig. 4a), indicating higher polarizability and stronger electroactivity under an electric field. At low temperatures (approximately −30 °C), both k and dielectric loss increased significantly (Supplementary Fig. 18a, d). This behavior resembles the polarization enhancement mechanism reported previously40. The structure in PVDF-SPF, referred to as loose β crystals (similar to intermediate phases), can greatly improve the reversible ECE. In contrast to terpolymers (Supplementary Fig. 18c, f), no dielectric peak was observed in PVDF-SPF at room temperature, suggesting the absence of conformational transitions41,42. The drop of k around 90 °C (Fig. 4a) illustrates structural relaxation and partial melting (Supplementary Fig. 15a), which may seriously reduce the ECE of PVDF-SPF.

Variable-temperature infrared spectra show a clear red shift in the characteristic peak of the long-β phase with increasing temperature, indicating weakened interchain dipole-dipole interactions (Supplementary Fig. 19a, c). Its absorbance gradually decreases and drops sharply above 80 °C, reflecting the strong temperature sensitivity of the long-β phase content. In contrast, the peak position and absorbance of the short-β phase remain nearly unchanged below 80 °C, which demonstrates its great thermal stability (Fig. 4b and Supplementary Fig. 19b). However, once the temperature exceeds 80 °C, a rapid decrease in the short-β phase is observed. This behavior indicates that 80 °C serves as a critical threshold for the structural stability of the short-β phase. Below this temperature, the β phase in PVDF-SPF remains stable without conformational transformation41. The structural evolution of β crystals was directly observed via variable-temperature 2D-WAXD (Supplementary Fig. 20). Around 80 °C, both crystal size and relative crystallinity exhibit inflection points. This indicates the β crystals undergo considerable thermal expansion accompanied by partial disintegration, which leads to a rapid decrease in relative crystallinity (Fig. 4c). A weak endothermic peak in the DSC curve also reflects this transition (Supplementary Fig. 15a). Before the collapse, the increased interchain spacing43 favors the ΔSorient.

In the range of 20–80 °C, the polarization difference (ΔP = Pmax − Pr) gradually increased (Fig. 4d and Supplementary Fig. 22). The resulting increase in ΔSdip led to a total ECE entropy change (ΔSECE) of 52.5 J kg−1 K−1 at 80 °C (Fig. 4e). This enhancement was attributed to tensileresidual stress (~15 MPa) introduced during the SPF process (Supplementary Fig. 23), which stabilized the loose β crystals and enabled a large ΔSorient below 80 °C. However, the ΔTECE of PVDF-SPF gradually decreased to 10.8 K at 80 °C (Supplementary Fig. 24a), due to the rapid increase in specific heat capacity (Supplementary Fig. 25) offsetting the gain in ΔSECE. Above 80 °C, the internal stress generated was gradually released. This induced molecular chain rearrangement and disorientation, along with partial melting of the loose β crystals. At high temperatures, the excessive thermal motion of molecular chains could not follow the electric field variation, and ΔSorient disappeared. At this point, the PVDF-SPF presented a high Pr and hysteresis loss (Supplementary Fig. 21), lowering the ΔSdip and ECE. Once the structure becomes unstable and collapses, the electrocaloric effect drops rapidly to nearly zero. The ΔSECE versus temperature curve of PVDF-SPF completely echoed the above variable-temperature tests, revealing an effective Tw of 60 °C for PVDF-SPF.

Considering the practical requirements for electrocaloric polymers, we selected five parameters: ΔTECE, Tw, Eb, Y, and Pmax as evaluation criteria (Supplementary Table 1). PVDF-SPF exhibited a large ΔTECE (12.8 K) and a high Pmax (9 μC cm−2), demonstrating significant potential for electrocaloric performance tuning. Its high Y (~1700 MPa) is expected to enhance the structural stability and operational durability of electrocaloric devices (Supplementary Fig. 26). Compared with previously reported electrocaloric materials (Supplementary Table 2), PVDF-SPF outperforms commercially available terpolymers in ΔTECE, ΔSECE, and Tw, highlighting its notable advantage in overall property balance (Fig. 4f). These results provide useful guidance for optimizing the trade-off between performance and fabrication in the design of future electrocaloric materials.

---

## Methods

Materials and general film preparation
PVDF powder (Solef® 5130) was purchased from Solvay S.A. with weight-average molecular weights (Mw) of 1000 kg mol−1. N, N-dimethylformamide (DMF, 99.9%) was obtained from Aladdin Biochemical Technology Co., Ltd. A 13 wt.% PVDF solution was prepared by dissolving 10 g of PVDF in 67 g of DMF. The solution was vigorously stirred for 12 h, then cast onto a smooth glass plate using a thick blade. The glass plate was placed in a vacuum oven at 80 °C for 24 h to obtain the PVDF-C film. The PVDF-C was cut into rectangular strips and stretched to a strain of 1400% at 85 °C using an electromechanical test system (Model E44, MTS Systems Co., Ltd.) to obtain the PVDF-S film.

Solid-phase pressure forming
The PVDF-S was clamped using adhesive gaskets (PTFE with single-sided tape, Taizhou Chenguang Plastic Industry Co., Ltd.) and placed in a hot press (R-3201, Wuhan Qien Science & Technology Development Co., Ltd.) at 85 °C. The pressure was gradually applied to 30 MPa within 2 min. Cooling water was then circulated to bring the film to room temperature, resulting in the PVDF-SPF film. This film was subsequently subjected to the same process at 155 °C to obtain the PVDF-SPF film. The process of solid-phase pressure forming primarily involves transverse expansion of the film, with slight change in the original stretching direction (Supplementary Fig. 18).

Microstructure characterization
Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR, Spectrum two, PerkinElmer Inc.) was employed to characterize the conformational composition of the samples with attenuated total reflection (ATR) accessory. The infrared spectra of the samples were collected using the ATR accessory with incident light parallel to the original stretching direction. For variable-angle infrared spectroscopy (VA-IR), the sample was placed at the center of the protractor, and infrared spectra were obtained in ATR mode at 15° intervals (Supplementary Note 3). For variable-temperature infrared spectroscopy, the sample was positioned on a custom temperature-controlled stage. The heating rate was 1–2 °C min−1, with measurements taken at 5 °C intervals. The temperature-controlled stage consisted of a temperature controller (TCM1030, Chengdu Yexian Technology Co., Ltd.), a polyimide heating plate (0402828, Yancheng Zhenglong Electric Heating Technology Co., Ltd.), and a platinum resistor (PT1000, Heraeus), which was positioned near the sample to monitor the temperature accurately. 2D wide-angle X-ray diffraction (Xeuss 3.0, Xenocs S.A.) with Cu/Kα radiation (wavelength 1.54189 Å) was performed to characterize the crystalline structure of the samples, with a pixel size of 75 μm. For variable-temperature WAXD, the temperature was controlled using a cooling-heating stage (HFSX350, Linkam), with a heating rate of 1–2 °C min−1 and measurements taken at 5 °C intervals. Thermal analysis was characterized using differential scanning calorimeter (DSC) (DSC25, TA Instruments) with a heating/cooling rate of 10 °C min−1. The conformational distribution and morphology of samples were conducted using tapping mode with pixel scan of 256 × 256 by atomic force microscopy equipped with infrared spectroscopy (AFM-IR, Dimension Icon IR, Bruker). The samples were excited with infrared light at 1275 cm−1 and scanned simultaneously. The Young’s modulus of the samples was measured using the same AFM.

Functional properties characterization
Permittivity spectroscopy was evaluated using a precision LCR meter (E4980A, Keysight Technologies) equipped with a temperature-controlled stage (same as the stage utilized in variable-temperature infrared spectroscopy). The heating rate was maintained at 1–2 °C min−1, with measurements taken at 2 °C intervals. Unipolar and bipolar ferroelectric hysteresis loops were measured by a ferroelectric tester (CPE1901, PolyK Technologies) with a modified Sawyer-Tower circuit at a frequency of 10 Hz. The electrostriction of PVDF-SPF was measured using a high-voltage amplifier equipped with a laser interferometer (SP-S120, SIOS Meßtechnik GmbH). DC breakdown strength was tested at a rate of 500 V s−1. Weibull analysis with two parameters was used to study the characteristic breakdown strength (Eb) of the samples18,

P(E) = 1 − exp (− (E/Eb)β) (2)

where E is the breakdown field of fifteen samples measured during the ferroelectric hysteresis test, Eb is the characteristic breakdown strength at 63.2% probability of breakdown, P(E) is the cumulative probability of breakdown, and β is the parameter related to film reliability. Unless otherwise stated, silver electrodes were sputtered on both sides of the films for all electrical measurements. The upper and lower electrodes had diameters of 6 mm and 8 mm, respectively, and their centers were aligned.

In-situ FTIR and 2D-WAXD characterization
For In situ high-voltage infrared spectroscopy (HV-IR), the sample surfaces were coated with carbon nanotubes (CNTs, Suzhou Tanfeng Technology Co., Ltd.). The film was positioned on a custom high-voltage sample stage (Supplementary Fig. 7), and an external high-voltage source (TCM6000i, Dalian Teslaman Technology Co., Ltd.) was used to apply the electric field. Spectra were measured in transmission mode. For in situ high-voltage 2D wide-angle X-ray diffraction (2DHV-WAXD), silver electrodes were sputtered on both sides of the film by a magnetron sputtering system (GVC-2000, Gevee Instruments Co., Ltd.). The film was then placed on the high-voltage sample stage, with other procedures following the same protocol as the HV-IR measurement. The thickness of the samples was limited to 10 μm.

Estimation of interchain distance and crystallite size
The interchain distance was estimated using Bragg’s law,

nλ = 2d sin θ (3)

where n is the diffraction order, λ is the X-ray wavelength, θ is the diffraction angle, and d is the interchain spacing. The crystallite size was calculated using the Scherrer equation

Lhkl = kλ / (β cos θ) (4)

where Lhkl represents the crystallite size perpendicular to the (hkl) plane, λ is the X-ray wavelength, θ is the Bragg angle, and β is the full width at half maximum (FWHM) of the specified peak44. The dimensionless shape factor k = 0.89 was adopted in this work.

ECE measurement
The ECE of the samples was captured using a heat flux sensor (HFS-5, OMEGA Engineering Inc.). A high-voltage amplifier (EEL1102.05, Electrical Energy Limited LLC) provided the required voltage, and data were collected using an oscilloscope (DHO914, RIGOL Technologies Co., Ltd.). The heating and cooling of the samples were directly observed using a high-precision infrared thermal imager (Testo SE & Co. KGaA). The time-resolved electrocaloric temperature change was measured using an infrared thermometer (CTlaser LT, Optris GmbH). Before infrared measurement, a layer of carbon nanotubes was sprayed onto the silver electrode surface to enhance the emissivity of film. The emissivity of the film (ε = 0.85) was measured using a dual-band emissometer (IR-2, Shanghai Institute of Technical Physics). The film thickness used for ECE measurement was approximately 10–15 μm. Detailed information is available in Supplementary Note 2.

Data availability
All data are available from the corresponding author upon request. Source data are provided with this paper.

### Reviewer 1

The article entitled ‘From negligible to giant electrocaloric effect of poly(vinylidene fluoride)’ by Y. Zhang et al investigates the enhancement of the electrocaloric effects (ECE) in poly(vinylidene fluoride) (PVDF) films through solid-phase pressure forming (SPF), and achieved a seemingly giant ECE of deltaT = -14.1 K near 25degC within a wide temperature window of 60 Kelvins. The figures of merit attractively surpass various existing electrocaloric materials. Most notably, while double hysteresis in the bipolar P(E) underpinning large ECEs is normally understood in the framework of phase transitions between a low-field antiferroelectric/paraelectric phase and a high-field ferroelectric phase, the double hysteresis in PVDF-SPF is attributed to another route via decoupling the long-range ferroelectric order. An ‘amorphous beta phase’ could be readily induced into crystalline/ferroelectric beta phase, during which large entropy change associated with polar orientation could be harnessed.
The work is thus scientifically and technically novel, and suitable for publications on Nature Communications if the following concerns on methodological weakness and data inconsistence could be addressed.
I suggest the authors to add in the supplementary section a schematic illustration of how VA-IR works and how the data for PVDF-SPF relates to the illustration in Fig 1a-c for easier understanding of the readers.
To properly measure the ECE using an IR imager, the authors should provide time-resolved thermal profiles, alike of what has been demonstrated for the heat flux method in Fig. S3a. The authors should also present cross-verification between the heat flux method and the IR imager method for deltaT at different electric field near room temperature (or at various temperatures).
It’s also better to consolidate the ECE by showing calibration of the IR imager. Comparison of the temperature of CNT-sprayed surface measured by IR imager and the temperature of the heat controller should be plotted in the vicinity of room temperature, to show that emission of the CNT-sprayed surface is reliable and free from interference of low-emission metallic electrode surface and background noise.
The authors observed that ‘the infrared absorption of both the long-beta phase (1275 cm-1) and the short-beta phase (837 cm-1) weakened’, while the electric field application is supposed to increase the fraction of long-beta phase, and ideally enhances absorption at 1275 cm-1. What leads to the decrease?
The authors noted that the drastic decrease of ECEs at 90 degC is attributed to the crystallization of the amorphous beta phase, presumably into the normal beta phase since large remanent polarization is observed above 90 degC. But there’s inconsistence between such a claim and the fact that no signals for crystallization, e.g. peaks, were observed in their DSC near 90 degC. The inconsistence also exists for temperature-dependent FT-IR data, where the authors observed that both short-beta phase and long-beta phase decreased uniformly with rising temperature, instead of noticing a trade-off between the normal and amorphous beta phase.
The claim that there’s a drop in dielectric constant at 90 degC relating to this crystallization is also not solid, given that this dielectric drop near 90 degC has been seen in the PVDF-C and PVDF-S samples which would not contain the amorphous beta-phase.
There’s also inconsistence between the polarization data and the thermal data. In Fig. S16, either the remnant polarization or the maximal polarization for PVDF-SPF increases with temperature, and it seems dP/dT is positive for all fields. Since the Maxwell relation defines that dP/dT = dS/dE, an inverse effect (deltaS>0 for field application, and hence field application generates temperature drop) instead of the observed conventional effect should arise. And such an inverse effect should be the most substantial above 90 degC given the larger dP/dT values. All these lead to a significant discrepancy against the thermal measurements presented in the rest of this work.

### Reviewer 2

In this study, the authors present pressed PVDF films that achieve an EC temperature change of up to 14.1 K at 25 °C and a temperature window of 60 °C. The authors claim that the PVDF films underwent substantial plastic deformation and extensive crystal fragmentation under 30 MPa solid-phase pressure, resulting in the formation of small, loosely packed beta crystal grains. It is always interesting to see the highly reversible polar responses from the conventional ferroelectric pvdf, the manuscript is therefore interesting. However, I still have some questions and comments that are related to the validation, novelty, and significance of the work.
1. The authors claimed that "forming loose and tiny β crystal grains", and "The giant ECE primarily originates from orientation entropy changes of molecular chains associated with the reversible transition between loose and compact β crystals", as if the tiny and compact polar structures leading to the large ECE is the key finding. However, recent reports in PVDF-based polymers have already demonstrated the point (see ref. 11). From a broader picture, it is well known that the smaller and compact polar structures would lead to a high dipolar response (see Nature,2017, 546, 391). Therefore, the interesting part of this work should be how to generate these polar structures "in PVDF". To this point, the ref. 40 (Nat. Commun., 2019, 10, 4535) should be cited in a clearer position in this manuscript compared to its current position. The ref. 40 utilized a similar hot press process to reduce the size of the polar structures, which is directly related to this work and should be discussed in the beginning of the manuscript. I have no idea why the authors cite the papers but are not willing to discuss their true findings.
2. From the data of the heat sensor, the pressed PVDF is too lossy, as we observed that a constant heat was generated under the electric field. The amount of heat generated exceeds the heat absorbed during the removal of the electric field. This significant heating effect can accumulate over time, making the material unsuitable for practical applications in refrigeration devices. The authors should provide a solution to reduce the heating effect significantly before discussing the possibility for practical use of the material. Or the authors should argue that the heating is insignificant in application.
3. The heat measurement of the cooling effect is questionable. Anything above the baseline should not be integrated into the cooling effect without further evidence. The authors should work carefully on the measurement. Even without any cooling effect from the ECE, the heating curve will reduce to the baseline due to the convection. Once the field is removed, how much area of the signal integration (parts above the baseline) is due to the convection or heat absorption of ECE is not clear. It is highly possible that the reported ECE is overrated.
4. The analysis of economic refrigeration capacity is unnecessary and misleading. At the current stage, EC technology, including the material and device, has not been deployed in any market. Only a handful of companies have the raw polymer powder for sale. Therefore, the price of the relaxor ferroelectric polymer is overly high because there is no market. However, the energy cost to produce monomers TrFE and CFE is similar to the VDF. The price of the relaxor ferroelectric polymer should not be too far from the PVDF unless the authors prove otherwise with the data from the fuorine chemical industry. The current high price is temporary and can be affected by many factors. According to Arkema, once there is a market, the price of their polymers will drop significantly. Also, the refrigeration capacity is field-dependent. There is no standard for how much field was applied in this comparison (Supplementary Table II).
Since there is no commercially available electrocaloric device, there is no point in introducing this value of economic refrigeration capacity. The "high" ERC is shortsighted and immature, indicating the lack of investigation of this work.

### Reviewer 3

This work reports giant ECE of up to 14.1 K at 25 °C from PVDF films prepared by solid-phase pressure forming (PVDF-SPF). If experimentally substantiated, the work would represent an important progress in the field. The manuscript extensively describes the structural characterization results and rationalizes these to high ECE. Additional experimental data are required on the characterization of the ECE and direct measurement of the adiabatic temperature change. Once these are furnished, the work would become acceptable for publication.
1. Provide experimental data of the temperature change measured with IR camera, and how the ECE varies with sample information such as different thicknesses. Thicker films produce larger heat flux and thus minimizes the impact by parasitic loss. Also provide charts to show the temperature change with time during sinusoidal or square wave voltage scans.
2. Does the PVDF-SPF film show any electrostrictive behavior (e.g. expanding in film area) when subjected to the electric field?
3. The authors state that the giant electrocaloric effect in PVDF-SPF originates from the entropy change associated with the reversible reorientation of the tiny β-crystal grains. This core statement of the paper is against the prevailing point of view stating that the non-polar to polar phase transition generates the largest entropy change and is the origin of the giant electrocaloric effect. The paraelectric phases also have larger interchain spacings compared to that of β-phase. The chain orientation of the paraelectric phases can also be very random. Therefore, the discussions from line 178 to 196 are not convincing enough.
4. In figure 2d, why do peaks for long β-phase (1275 cm-1) and short β-phase (837 cm-1) both get weakened, but there is no intensity increase in any characteristic peak for the newly formed compact β-phase at 200MV/m? In fact, the compact β-phase is still β-phase. Is there any characteristic peak in the full FTIR spectrum for the compact β-phase formed at a high field?
5. Figure 2e shows the adiabatic temperature change (ΔT) versus the field strength for the PVDF-SPF film. The ΔT is calculated from the data measured by a heat flux sensor. The curve does not show any platform but a large increasing rate even if the field is increased up to 200MV/m, and the breakdown strength of 617 MV/m is still far above the maximum test field. Does this mean that ΔT still has a large room to be increased if the field is higher than 200MV/m?
6. The 14.1K of ΔT at 200MV/m calculated from the heat flux sensor measurement is a very large number. How does this compare to the ΔT measured using an IR camera under the same condition?
7. Figure 2e shows that the ΔT of PVDF-SPF is almost negligible at 50-80MV/m. To get a ΔT (at least 3-4 K) for practical cooling applications, the field needs to be at least 100MV/m which is not ideal for cooling device development. How does the ΔT scale with film thickness? From the material standpoint, provide potential approaches to obtain large ΔT at <100 MV/m.

### Reviewer 5

This paper presents an enhanced electrocaloric effect (ECE) in poly(vinylidene fluoride) (PVDF) homopolymer subjected to solid-state pressure forming. Given the low cost and wide availability of PVDF homopolymer, the reported findings are noteworthy and have the potential to stimulate further research of ECE in PVDF homopolymer.
